It looks like Tor just lost all credibility, and is now probably infested with cancer.

Tor is open-source with a BSD license, so its code can be examined and forked if need be.

Unfortunately i don't think it is so simple. TOR is not just a normal piece of code that anyone with some coding skills can understand and improve. You also need to be an expert in cryptography and security to understand the choices that the original developers have done and to not break its security by mistake... and this set of skills is much rarer.

Think about ReiserFS... it was quite a good filesystem that i have used for years without one issue and many users preferred it to ext3. Even in the worst conditions much of the data from ReiserFS could be restored without a byte lost and there were some exciting improvements planned for future releases. Yet, when Reiser, the original developer of ReiserFS went to jail (he apparently killed his wife), the project pretty much was abandoned to itself. Yes, someone took it over to make sure future versions of Linux would still be able to use it, but the whole community and developers behind it kept shrinking since then. None of the cool features promised by Reiser have been implemented since his legal troubles.

This just to show you that even if a project is opensource and it has lots of users it doesn't automatically mean that there will be someone interested enough and/or skilled/knowledgeable enough to take it over if the original head behind it is... beheaded. TOR in particular is a real pain in the ass, not only because it requires lots of knowledge and skills to develop it, but also because there are lots of bad players very interested in derailing it (think about NSA sockpuppets inside the developer community more than willing to sabotage the security of the project) and it can be the source of various legal problems that no one really wants.
